name: Tree Operations
description: This really says a lot about our society. One day, a turtle gives you a tree with $$$n$$$ nodes rooted at node $$$x$$$. Each node has an initial nonnegative value; the $$$i$$$-th node has starting value $$$a_i$$$. You want to make the values of all nodes equal to $$$0$$$. To do so, you will perform a series of operations on the tree, where each operation will be performed on a certain node. Define an operation on node $$$u$$$ as choosing a single node in $$$u$$$'s subtree$$$^{\text{∗}}$$$ and incrementing or decrementing its value by $$$1$$$. The order in which operations are performed on nodes is as follows: For $$$1 \le i \le n$$$, the $$$i$$$-th operation will be performed on node $$$i$$$. For $$$i \gt n$$$, the $$$i$$$-th operation will be performed on the same node as operation $$$i - n$$$. More formally, the $$$i$$$-th operation will be performed on the $$$(((i - 1) \bmod n) + 1)$$$-th node.$$$^{\text{†}}$$$ Note that you cannot skip over operations; that is, you cannot perform the $$$i$$$-th operation without first performing operations $$$1, 2, \ldots, i - 1$$$. Find the minimum number of operations you must perform before you can make the values of all nodes equal to $$$0$$$, assuming you pick operations optimally. If it's impossible to make the values of all nodes equal to $$$0$$$ after finite operations, output $$$-1$$$. $$$^{\text{∗}}$$$The subtree of a node $$$u$$$ is the set of nodes for which $$$u$$$ lies on the shortest path from this node to the root, including $$$u$$$ itself. $$$^{\text{†}}$$$Here, $$$a \bmod b$$$ denotes the remainder from dividing $$$a$$$ by $$$b$$$.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1\le t\le 100$$$) — the number of test cases. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$x$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 2000$$$, $$$1 \le x \le n$$$) — the number of nodes and the root of the tree. The second line of each test case contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$0 \le a_i \le 10^9$$$) — the starting value of each node. Each of the next $$$n - 1$$$ lines of each test case contains two integers $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$ ($$$1 \le u, v \le n$$$, $$$u \neq v$$$) representing an undirected edge from $$$u$$$ to $$$v$$$. It is guaranteed that the given edges form a tree. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$2000$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, output a single integer denoting the minimum amount of operations needed to make all nodes $$$0$$$. If it's impossible to make all nodes $$$0$$$, output $$$-1$$$.
approach_summary: Define tree DP state dp[u][state] computing optimal subproblem values for the subtree rooted at u. Aggregate transitions across children in post-order traversal in O(N × S) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2035F — Tree Operations [463. DP on Trees and DAGs]
topic_editorial.summary: Tree Dynamic Programming with post-order traversal.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: A rooted tree has a clean hierarchical structure: removing the root decomposes the tree into independent disjoint subtrees. Therefore, the optimal solution for a subtree rooted at vertex $u$ depends purely on the solutions of its direct children $v \in \text{children}(u)$.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Root Selection & State Definition
Arbitrarily root the tree at node $1$. Define:
- $dp[u][0] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is excluded.
- $dp[u][1] = $ optimal value for the subtree of $u$ if node $u$ is included.

### Step 2: Post-Order DFS Traversal
We traverse the tree using depth-first search. A node $u$ computes its answers only after all its children $v \in \text{adj}[u]$ have computed theirs:
$$\text{dfs}(u, \text{parent})$$

### Step 3: Subtree Transition
For each child $v$ of $u$ ($v \ne \text{parent}$):
$$dp[u][0] = \sum_{v} \max(dp[v][0], dp[v][1])$$
$$dp[u][1] = \text{val}[u] + \sum_{v} dp[v][0]$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
At the root:
$$\text{Ans} = \max(dp[1][0], dp[1][1])$$
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Each node and edge in the tree is visited exactly once during the DFS traversal. All transitions at node $u$ run in time proportional to its degree. Summing across all vertices: $\sum \text{deg}(u) = 2(N-1) = \mathcal{O}(N)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  Adjacency list storage takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, DP state arrays take $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, and the DFS call stack takes at most $\mathcal{O}(N)$ depth in the worst case.
